Just a friendly warning to anyone reading your edit: Make sure to not go overboard with your DPI setting. Comfortable aiming across all distances in a first person shooter - from casually flickshotting in close quarters combat to finely adjusting your aim while sniping - should take priority. An overly-high DPI won't do anyone good if you try to aim for a headshot but the settings are so maxed out that your crosshairs jumps over your target's head.

Alternatively you can buy a mouse that can swap between multiple DPI modes so that you have responsive mouse speed while unscoped and at the press of a button you can prepare yourself to snipe with a decreased DPI threshold - but I personally prefer consistency across the board when it comes to DPI.

Like with running/track shoes, get something that will fit you - not something that's so small/big because someone else has it that it'll cramp your style (and your joints).

General rule of thumb: Sensor quality over DPI count. Look around for community talk about what mouse has great/amazing optical sensors (my current mouse has a Pixart PMW 3366 - quite possibly the best afaik) and get one in combination with a nice big mouse mat to help with those flickshots.

Next time you're gaming with a mouse, check the way you're holding it. Are you palming it (ie: no under-finger gaps)? Get a mouse that's relatively flat to reduce strain. Claw grip (ie: your fingertips are poised on the buttons)? Get a mouse with a high arching back for a better grip.

Good palm grip mice: Logitech G900 Zowie (almost all Zowie mice share the same shell)

Good claw grip mice: Razer DeathAdder (the only Razer product I'd personally recommend) NOTE: Avoid the Chroma (bad laser sensor) SteelSeries (like with the Zowie, they use similar shapes)

Make sure that you don't buy a mouse that's too small, of course. Check the dimensions of the products and ask around - otherwise the aforementioned mice/brands should serve you well if you're unsure of what to get when it comes to getting something ergonomic.

Your follow-up purchase should be a good mechanical keyboard. If you don't have to worry about waking up anyone (and like loud clicky keys), get a keyboard with Cherry MX Blue switches. Otherwise if you'll be recording while playing games, get its quieter (but no less responsive) Cherry MX Brown cousin as a good mechanical keyboard can reduce or even eliminate typing fatigue (I suffer from hypermobility and all the RSI/joint strain that comes with it - ever since typing with a mechanical keyboard I haven't been in serious bouts of post-document-typing handcramp pain).

TL;DR: focus on getting one with a good sensor. Buy a mechanical keyboard too.
